The salt had eaten the brass fittings long ago, leaving them green and pitted like old teeth. Elias didn’t mind. He liked the decay. It meant time was still moving, even here, at the edge of the world where the Atlantic gnawed at the granite foundations of the tower.

Every night, Elias climbed the one hundred and forty-four steps. His knees cracked in protest, a dry, wooden sound that echoed in the spiral stairwell. At the top, the Fresnel lens waited, a cathedral of glass and prisms. He polished it with a chamois cloth, his breath fogging the cold air. The beam swept out, a golden finger pointing into the dark, cutting through the fog that rolled in from the sea like a living thing.

He wasn’t lonely. He was solitary. There was a difference. Loneliness was a hole in the chest; solitude was a room with the door closed. In this room, Elias kept the light. He kept the rhythm. Three seconds dark, three seconds light. *Blink. Blink.* It was the heartbeat of the coast. Ships passed in the distance, tiny sparks of warning, trusting the beam to keep them from the rocks.
